To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Lp(a) is a major immunogenic lipoprotein in normal human plasma and that its apo(a) subunits are the major antigenic determinants of circulating Lp (a) immune complexes.
Lp(a) immune complexes of varying particle density contain IgG and are liberated from plasma lipoprotein fraction by melibiose.
anti-Gal, a major antibody of the IgG class present in plasma of normal individuals, binds to the O-glycosylated serine- and thrreonine-rich peptide region of apo(a) in Lp(a).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of apo(a) O-glycans in Lp(a)-specific IC formation.
a new mechanism of Lp(a)-mediated atherosclerosis and thrombosis, which involves the interaction of anti-Gal and STPS in apo(a).
the formation of Lp(a)-IC by anti-Gal and the role of O-linked oligosaccharides in the interaction of Lp(a), atherogenic lipoprotein, with plasma antibodies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
anti-Gal binds STPS in apo(a) subunits of Lp(a).
anti-Gal antibody recognizes STPS in O–glycan-rich regions of Lp(a).
anti-Gal is a natural autoantibody which binds to STPS of apo(a) and that Lp(a) is the natural antigen for this antibody in plasma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Lp(a) is the most potent inhibitor of the lectin-mediated immune reaction and that the immune response to this lipoprotein is directed against STPS.
anti-Gal binds to STPS in apo(a) subunits of circulating Lp (a) and that the binding of Lp(a), in turn, induces conformational changes in the Fc portion of the antibody.
the anti-Gal-Lp(a) interaction involves a novel mechanism of antibody-antigen interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the apo(a) subunits of circulating Lp (a)-anti-Gal complexes have a conformation that is different from those in the native Lp(a) particle and that this conformational shift is due to the binding of the antibody to the STPS region of the apo(a) molecule.
the STPS in the N-terminal domain of apo(a) is a target for circulating antibodies and that Lp(a) is an important antigen for anti-Gal.
apo(a) subunits of circulating Lp (a) are not glycosylated with α-galactose.
